ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Restore restaurant-level (four-wall) EBITDA margin toward the prior ~19% range without sacrificing traffic, value positioning, or service speed/quality. CEO must decide before the next franchise/lender review (~60-90 days) whether to re-engineer the unit model, take additional price, or slow new-unit growth. A lender covenant is tied to restaurant-level margin.
ownerConstraints: Competitive pricing cap: Menu pricing power is limited by aggressive value competition; broad price increases beyond ~2% risk traffic loss and have historically been offset roughly 1:1 by traffic decline.

Franchise / brand standards constraint: Menu, portion, packaging, and operating procedures are governed by brand standards; unit-level changes cannot violate brand consistency or quality specifications.
Minimum wage law constraint: A meaningful share of crew labor is at or near statutory minimum wage in multiple jurisdictions; wage floors are rising and cannot be reduced below legal minimums.
Value-menu commitments: Public value-menu / promotional price commitments restrict the ability to re-price entry-level items in the near term.
Speed and quality constraint: Cannot degrade drive-thru/service speed or food quality; throughput and quality are core to traffic and same-store sales, so labor cuts that slow service are off-limits.
Covenant constraint: Lender covenant tied to restaurant-level margin limits actions that would further depress near-term four-wall profitability.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Unit-level profitability is declining even though system revenue is stable. Same-store sales are flat (0%) while food costs rose ~8% and labor costs rose ~10%, compressing restaurant-level EBITDA margin from 19% to 15%. The operator cannot price its way out (competition caps menu increases at ~2%, and that increase was already offset by a 2% traffic decline). The CEO must determine whether the margin erosion is a pricing-structure problem, a demand/traffic problem, or a fundamental four-wall unit-economics problem, ahead of a covenant-relevant lender/franchise review in the next 60-90 days.

businessProblem: A 200+ unit company-operated QSR chain with ~$850M of system revenue (AUV ~$4.25M) is experiencing declining unit-level profitability despite stable system revenue. Same-store sales are flat (0% YoY): the operator took +2% of menu price, but it was fully offset by a -2% traffic decline, so there is no top-line offset to absorb cost inflation. Meanwhile food & paper (COGS) cost inflation ran +8% and labor cost inflation ran +10% (rising minimum wages plus scheduling/overtime pressure). As a result, food & paper rose from 28.0% to 30.0% of sales and labor rose from 30.0% to 32.0% of sales, while occupancy (9%) and other opex (14%) held. Restaurant-level EBITDA margin therefore fell from 19.0% to 15.0%, a 400 bps decline (~$170k of EBITDA per unit, ~$34M across the system). The core challenge: Is this a pricing-structure error (the menu is mispriced), a demand-forecasting/traffic problem (the chain mis-read demand), or a four-wall unit-economics breakdown (the per-unit cost of output has outrun sustainable contribution)? Pricing power is capped by competition and value-menu commitments; cutting labor risks slowing service and further eroding traffic and SSS. The CEO must decide—before a covenant-relevant lender/franchise review in 60-90 days—whether to re-engineer the unit model, take additional price, or slow new-unit growth.

evidence.finding: Restaurant-level EBITDA margin declined from 19.0% (prior year) to 15.0% (FY2025), a 400 basis point compression, on flat same-store sales (0% YoY). At an AUV of $4.25M, this is a ~$170k per-unit decline in restaurant-level EBITDA (from ~$807.5k to $637.5k), or roughly $34M across the 200-unit system. Because same-store sales are flat, the entire 400 bps of margin decline is attributable to cost-line deterioration, not volume.
evidence.source: SEC EDGAR 10-K restaurant-level (non-GAAP) margin disclosure and investor-presentation AUV reporting (QSR pattern)

evidence.finding: Food & paper (COGS) rose from 28.0% to 30.0% of sales (+200 bps) and labor rose from 30.0% to 32.0% of sales (+200 bps). Combined, the two cost lines account for +400 bps of margin drag—exactly the observed restaurant-level margin decline—because same-store sales are flat and occupancy (9%) and other opex (14%) held constant. The drivers are food cost inflation of ~+8% and labor wage inflation of ~+10% (minimum-wage increases plus scheduling/overtime).
evidence.source: SEC EDGAR 10-K restaurant-level P&L cost-line disclosure and commodity/wage cost commentary (QSR pattern)

evidence.finding: The operator took +2% of menu price in FY2025, but same-store sales were flat (0%) because a -2% traffic decline fully offset the price increase. Pricing power is capped by aggressive value competition and existing value-menu commitments, so additional broad price increases risk further traffic loss rather than incremental margin. There is therefore no realistic top-line lever to absorb the +8% food and +10% labor inflation in the near term.
evidence.source: Investor-presentation SSS bridge (price vs traffic) and competitive value-menu commentary (QSR pattern)

evidence.finding: Because the food and labor cost lines are reported only in aggregate (% of sales) and not split into theoretical-vs-actual food cost (waste/over-portioning) or labor-deployment efficiency, it is not yet possible to attribute the +200 bps food drag and +200 bps labor drag between pure input inflation and controllable unit-level inefficiency. Unit-by-unit dispersion across the 200 restaurants is also undisclosed, so a representative-sample four-wall diagnostic is required before any system-wide remedy.
evidence.source: Gap between public aggregate cost-line disclosure and unit-level operational detail (QSR pattern)
